title: Motional EMF: Polarity, Numericals, Rotating Rod, and Energy Consideration

claims.text: Finding which end of a rod moving through a magnetic field becomes positive/negative: a rod (made of many positive and negative charges) moves with velocity v through field B. Using F=qv x B on the positive charges, force accumulates positive charge at one end (say A) and negative at the other (B). As charges accumulate, they set up their own electric field opposing further accumulation; equilibrium is reached when the electric force FE equals the magnetic force FM on the charges. The rod then behaves as if a fictitious battery is connected across it (though no battery is actually there -- it is charge separation), giving the direction of the motional EMF

Worked numerical (jet plane in Earth's magnetic field): a jet plane, wingspan (length) l=25 m, flies west at v=1800 km/hr. Only the Earth's HORIZONTAL field component BH (not the vertical component BV, since BV is parallel to the wing length l and so contributes nothing -- all three of v, l, and B must be mutually perpendicular for motional EMF) is relevant, since BH is perpendicular to both v and l. Given B=5x10^-4 T and angle of dip delta=30 degrees, BH = B cos(delta) = 5x10^-4 x (root3/2). EMF = BH x l x v (v converted to m/s via x5/18). Polarity found the same way as above (F=qv x B on positive charges) -- for this configuration, wingtip A comes out negative and B positive

EMF induced due to rotation of a conductor in a uniform magnetic field: a rod of length l, hinged at one end (centre) and free at the other, rotates with angular velocity omega in a uniform field B (parallel to the rotation axis). Considering the small EMF contributed by an element of the rod and integrating (calculus setup: d(flux) over dt), the total EMF between the centre and the outer end works out to epsilon = (1/2) B omega l^2

Worked numerical (rotating rod): a metallic rod of length 1 m is rotated at a frequency of 50 rev/s, one end hinged at the centre, the other end at the circumference of a circular metallic ring of radius 1 m, about an axis through the centre perpendicular to the ring's plane. A uniform field B=1 T is parallel to the axis everywhere. Find the EMF between the centre and the ring. Solution: omega=2*pi*nu=2*pi*50 rad/s; epsilon=(1/2)*B*omega*l^2=(1/2)(1)(2*pi*50)(1)^2=50*pi volts

Second worked numerical (started on the board, NCERT-style): a wheel with 10 metallic spokes, each 0.5 m long, is rotated at 120 rev/min in a plane normal to the horizontal component of Earth's magnetic field HE at a place, where HE=0.4 gauss

Energy consideration in a motional-EMF circuit: a conducting rod ab (length l) slides with velocity v on rails cd, connected via a resistor R, in field B. EMF epsilon=Blv, current i=Blv/R. The magnetic force on the current-carrying rod is Fm=BIl=B^2l^2v/R, directed opposite to v (by Fleming's left-hand rule / F=I(l x B), consistent with Lenz's law). To keep the rod moving at constant velocity, an external applied force F=B^2l^2v/R (equal and opposite to Fm) must be supplied. The rate at which this applied force does work is P_applied = F*v = B^2l^2v^2/R. The rate at which electrical energy is dissipated in the circuit is P_dissipated = I^2*R = (Blv/R)^2*R = B^2l^2v^2/R. Since these are equal, P_applied=P_dissipated -- confirming energy conservation: the mechanical work done in pushing the rod is exactly converted into electrical energy dissipated in the resistor

markdown_body:
## Motional EMF: polarity, and worked numericals (NCERT 6.6)

**Finding polarity:** for a rod moving with velocity $v$ through field $B$, using $\vec F=q\vec v\times\vec B$ on the rod's free charges, positive charge accumulates at one end and negative at the other, until the resulting internal electric field balances the magnetic force ($F_E=F_M$ at equilibrium). The rod then behaves like a fictitious battery — no battery is actually present, only charge separation.

### Worked numerical: jet plane in Earth's field
A jet, wingspan $l=25$ m, flies west at $v=1800$ km/hr. Only Earth's **horizontal** field component $B_H$ matters (the vertical component $B_V$ is parallel to $l$, so contributes nothing — $v$, $l$, $B$ must all be mutually perpendicular). With $B=5\times10^{-4}$ T, dip angle $\delta=30°$:
$$B_H = B\cos\delta = 5\times10^{-4}\times\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$$
$$\varepsilon = B_H\, l\, v \qquad (v \text{ in m/s, via} \times 5/18)$$
Polarity found the same way as above via $\vec F=q\vec v\times\vec B$.

## EMF from a rotating conductor

A rod of length $l$, hinged at the centre and free at the other end, rotates with angular velocity $\omega$ in a uniform field $B$ parallel to the rotation axis:
$$\boxed{\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2}B\omega l^2}$$

**Worked numerical:** rod length $1$ m, rotated at $50$ rev/s, hinged at the centre of a ring of radius $1$ m, $B=1$ T parallel to the axis. $\omega=2\pi\nu=2\pi(50)$ rad/s:
$$\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2}(1)(2\pi\times50)(1)^2 = 50\pi~\text{V}$$

**Second numerical (setup):** a wheel with $10$ metallic spokes, each $0.5$ m long, rotated at $120$ rev/min in a plane normal to Earth's horizontal field $H_E=0.4$ gauss.

## Energy consideration in motional EMF (NCERT 6.6)

Conducting rod $ab$ (length $l$) slides with velocity $v$ on rails, closed through resistance $R$, in field $B$:
$$\varepsilon = Blv, \qquad i = \frac{Blv}{R}$$
Magnetic force on the current-carrying rod, opposing $v$ (Lenz's law / Fleming's left-hand rule):
$$F_m = BIl = \frac{B^2l^2v}{R}$$
To keep the rod moving at **constant velocity**, an equal and opposite applied force $F=B^2l^2v/R$ is needed. Rate of work done by this applied force:
$$P_\text{applied} = Fv = \frac{B^2l^2v^2}{R}$$
Rate of electrical energy dissipated in the circuit:
$$P_\text{dissipated} = I^2R = \left(\frac{Blv}{R}\right)^2 R = \frac{B^2l^2v^2}{R}$$
$$\boxed{P_\text{applied} = P_\text{dissipated}}$$
confirming energy conservation: mechanical work done pushing the rod converts exactly into dissipated electrical energy.
